hero.headline: A founder dispute fought as a charitable-trust case.
hero.deck: Twenty-six causes of action have collapsed to three live liability theories. The fight is no longer the full founding saga — it is whether the 2015 founding emails, charter, and solicitations created an enforceable charitable trust, whether the OpenAI defendants must disgorge benefits retained from Musk's funding, and whether Microsoft knowingly assisted any breach.

executive_summary.title: What this case is actually about
executive_summary.thesis: Stripped of the rhetoric about looted charities, captured Microsofts, and AI extinction, the liability trial is a charitable-trust and restitution dispute between founders, with Microsoft exposed only on aiding-and-abetting. Dkt #497 removed fraud and constructive fraud with prejudice; the jury and the Court (on the equitable counts) are left with trust formation, breach, restitution, limitations, and Microsoft's knowledge or substantial assistance. The trial record has produced two pieces of evidence that materially shape those questions: Greg Brockman's contemporaneous personal journal (PX 151, 154, 161, 163; DX 1252) and Robert Wu's OpenAI 30(b)(6) deposition fixing the for-profit waterfall at roughly $250B in target redemptions before the nonprofit residual is paid.

components.title: Control dispute
components.description: The proximate cause of the 2017 breakdown is documented in the negotiation emails and now in Brockman's journal: Musk demanded 'unequivocal initial control' of any for-profit OpenAI, the founders refused, and by November 5, 2017 (DX 1252) Brockman wrote 'Real decision is fire Elon … So we seem converged on the Fire Elon route.' Plaintiffs frame the same period as a 'morally bankrupt' plan to convert the nonprofit; defendants frame it as a control fight Musk lost and walked away from. Both sides need this exchange and neither names it the central fact, because the jury treating the case as a control dispute rather than a charity dispute hurts each.
components.weight: Heavy — sourced to the September 20, 2017 Sutskever/Brockman email, Musk's trial admission of seeking 'unequivocal control', and Brockman's contemporaneous journal entries from August and November 2017.

components.title: Market-positioning dispute
components.description: OpenAI's counterclaim frames the lawsuit as competitive interference by xAI; the timing of the August 2024 filing (after xAI was capitalized) and the February 2025 $97.4B letter of intent fit that frame. Plaintiffs deny it, but Musk's testimony — xAI has no profit caps, he controls it, it converted from B-corp to C-corp — is in the record under oath, and the LOI exhibits (DX 1156, DX 1157) are admitted.
components.weight: Significant — sourced to OpenAI Counterclaim ¶6, ¶70, and Musk's cross-examination on xAI's structure and the LOI.

components.title: Mission dispute
components.description: The lead live claim is charitable trust, and the underlying question — whether the 2015 founding emails, charter language, solicitations, and donations created a public-benefit obligation enforceable by Musk — is the legal hinge. The Court, in the PI denial, called the existence of an enforceable trust a 'toss-up'. The trial record has tilted that question. Brockman's PX 161 journal entry, written while OpenAI was publicly committing to the nonprofit, reads: 'Cannot say that we are committed to the nonprofit. Don't wanna say that we're committed if three months later we're doing B Corp, then it was a lie' — and 'it'd be wrong to steal the nonprofit from him. To convert to B Corp without him. They'd be pretty morally bankrupt.' That is OpenAI's sitting president, in 2017, characterizing the contemplated path in the language plaintiffs now use.
components.weight: Contested but tilted by the trial record — the journal entries put contemporaneous internal-to-OpenAI evidence into the case that the parties' MSJ briefing did not have.

components.title: Microsoft knowledge
components.description: Microsoft's defense is that the partnership was arm's-length and that it had no actual knowledge of any Musk-specific trust duty. The 2023 Joint Development & Commercialization Agreement licensed Microsoft 'all IP and technology … excluding only AGI', and the non-binding Watershed MOU would let Microsoft reach product IP after a third-party panel determines that AGI has been achieved. The deliberate AGI carve-out, and Microsoft's negotiated path to claw it back, is direct circumstantial evidence that Microsoft understood the AGI restriction was load-bearing for OpenAI's original mission.
components.weight: Heavy — sourced to Robert Wu's 30(b)(6) deposition (Day 7), the 2023 JDCA terms, and the Watershed MOU description.

components.title: Remedy dispute
components.description: A late and consequential fight: who, if anyone, can receive a remedy. Musk has waived any personal award and asked to redirect relief to the OpenAI charity. Defendants argue that move exposes a no-personal-injury/no-remedy problem under California restitution law, where the recovery runs to the plaintiff. Wu's testimony fixed the size of what would be at stake on the equitable side: roughly $250B in aggregate target redemption ahead of the nonprofit residual, escalating 20% per year from 2025; Microsoft's 2023 round at a $60B / 6× target.
components.weight: Heavy — sourced to Dkts #484, #491, #492, the May 1 jury-instructions colloquy, and the Wu 30(b)(6) deposition.

components.title: Personal grievance
components.description: Musk's three-phase narrative ('enthusiastic, uncertain, looting') is structured around a personal sense of betrayal that the Court has treated as orthogonal to the legal question. Defense's 'tale of two Elons' and 'pageant of hypocrisy' tropes treat the same emotion as motive evidence. Brockman's Day 7 narration — 'I will withhold funding until you decide what you're going to do' — confirms the personal-grievance dynamic was real and contemporaneous on both sides.

sections.title: What each side is actually fighting over.
sections.deck: Stated motives ('AI safety,' 'the original mission,' 'humanity') against revealed motives in the documentary record.

blocks.text: Musk's stated motive is to recover a charity that has been 'looted' and converted into an $840B for-profit empire (post-money valuation surfaced on Day 6). His revealed motive — visible across the contemporaneous emails (DX 773, DX 749, DX 853), his August 2017 demand for 'unequivocal initial control', his September 2020 'captured by Microsoft' tweet, his Sept 2017 alternate proposal of 'a standard C corp with a parallel nonprofit', and his February 2025 $97.4B LOI for OpenAI's assets — is harder to fix on a single point. The record is consistent with at least two readings: a man genuinely outraged at the betrayal of a public trust, and a man positioned competitively against a rival he founded and then quit.

OpenAI's stated motive is to defend a mission-driven restructuring forced by the capital intensity of frontier AI. Its revealed motive in the counterclaims is to fight off a 'years-long harassment campaign' driven by a competitor it cannot tolerate seeing succeed. Both readings are present in the documents the defense itself filed (Counterclaim ¶6, ¶70). The court has accepted at the pleading stage that both readings can coexist. The trial record adds a third element the briefing did not: Brockman's contemporaneous internal-to-OpenAI journal, which describes the contemplated B Corp conversion as something it would be 'morally bankrupt' to do without Musk and which writes that publicly committing to the nonprofit would be 'a lie' if a B Corp followed in three months.

Microsoft's stated motive is the disciplined defense of an arm's-length partnership where it 'did not receive a conventional equity ownership interest.' Its revealed leverage — disclosed by Musk's testimony, the November 2023 board episode, OpenAI's Azure dependence, and Robert Wu's 30(b)(6) deposition — is economic and licensing leverage rather than conventional equity. Wu put numbers on the stack: roughly $250B in aggregate target redemptions before the nonprofit residual is paid; Microsoft's 2023 round at a $60B / 6× target; a 20% annual escalator from 2025; the 2023 JDCA license to 'all IP and technology … excluding only AGI'; and the non-binding Watershed MOU under which Microsoft would receive 'certain access to certain product IP' after a third-party panel determines AGI has been achieved. Microsoft's proposed findings still contest the legal elements: actual knowledge of a Musk-specific trust, substantial assistance, limitations, laches, and unclean hands. The deliberate AGI carve-out in the JDCA, and the Watershed MOU's negotiated path to reach it, are the cleanest evidence on the actual-knowledge element of aiding and abetting.
What the trier of fact is actually deciding

Three liability questions. First, do the 2015 founding emails, the charter, the solicitations, and the donations create an enforceable charitable trust whose corpus is the institution OpenAI became? Second, did the OpenAI defendants unjustly retain Musk-funded benefits such that restitution is available — and did the contributions Musk made through donor-advised funds and YC.org confer Musk personally with settlor standing? Third, did Microsoft have actual knowledge of the trust duties and substantially assist a breach? Remedy follows later: PTO #3 (#456) assigns disgorgement to the Court as an equitable remedy; PTO #4 (#477) bifurcates liability and remedies; and Dkts #484, #491, #492 tee up whether Musk can disclaim a personal award and still obtain relief for the OpenAI charity, against the California restitution rule that recovery runs to the plaintiff.

sections.title: How Musk's camp constructs its narrative.

blocks.text: The plaintiffs' through-line is moral: 'You can't steal a charity.' Molo's opening invoked the museum-store metaphor. Musk's testimony returned to the 'three phases' (enthusiastic, uncertain, looting) and the 'stolen car' analogy. Brockman's Day 6-7 journal testimony now gives plaintiffs contemporaneous language for the same frame: 'steal the nonprofit,' 'morally bankrupt,' 'then it was a lie,' and 'get out from under Elon.' The hard moral framing serves four functions: it activates jurors' priors about charitable abuse; it personifies the dispute; it suppresses inconvenient details; and it converts a contractual question into a question about American philanthropy itself.

The sympathetic witnesses are deliberately compact. Musk himself dominates the case-in-chief; Birchall authenticates the donation chart; Stuart Russell and David Schizer arrive late to provide expert framing on AI risk and on charitable-trust law. Plaintiffs declined to call Sam Altman in their case-in-chief — a choice that telegraphs they prefer the defense to handle Altman themselves.

Downplayed: Musk's 2017 'C corp with a parallel nonprofit' email; his 2018 'attach to Tesla as its cash cow' exchange (DX 749); his 'OK by me' on the cap-50× corporate proposal (DX 806); his 2020 'last penny' admission; xAI's lack of profit caps. The plaintiffs' opening barely engaged any of these; the cross-examination forced each into the record. The strategy was to keep the moral frame load-bearing and let the cross do its damage to the periphery.

sections.title: How OpenAI's camp constructs its narrative.

blocks.text: OpenAI's through-line is character: 'pageant of hypocrisy.' Savitt's opening built the contradiction structure — Musk demands control, leaves when he doesn't get it, pledges $1B and contributes $38M, attacks the institution he built when his rival fails to overtake it. Each piece is documented: the September 2017 control fight, Birchall's 'zero' answer for Brockman, the cross-examination accountancy of the $1B pledge, the Tesla 'attach' email, xAI's structure, and the LOI as a sham bid. Day 7 added the defense's journal answer: DX 1252's 'fire Elon route' came in as a prior consistent statement to argue that 'morally bankrupt' was about removing Musk from the board and then forming a B Corp without him, not conversion itself.

The sympathetic witnesses are technical and procedural. Nadella appears not to defend Microsoft from a corporate-control narrative but to deny the technical premise — there is no conventional equity, the partnership was arm's-length. Sutskever's 14-page declaration anchors the technical compute argument that drove the 2018–2019 capital change. The defense lets Musk be his own worst witness.

Downplayed: the magnitude of the for-profit's value relative to the nonprofit; Microsoft's role in the November 2023 board crisis; and insider economics. The trial has now surfaced some of what the redacted MSJ record obscured: Brockman's approximate $30B stake acquired for $0, the $10M Altman side arrangement described in PX-350, and Wu's target-redemption stack. The remaining unknowns are still substantial, but the public trial record is no longer limited to redacted briefing.

sections.title: Greg Brockman's journal as the central document.
sections.deck: The only contemporaneous internal-to-OpenAI document in evidence that addresses honesty and motive in 2017–2018.

blocks.text: Brockman has kept a personal journal on his laptop since 2010. Approximately 460 pages were produced in discovery; roughly 100 of those cover the August–September 2017 negotiation window. Plaintiffs put four entries in evidence as PX 151, 154, 161, and 163; the defense added a fifth, DX 1252, on Day 7. Every other contemporaneous communication from that period is either an email between Musk and the founders (where the founders were addressing Musk directly) or a public-facing artifact (the charter, blog posts, IRS filings). The journal is Brockman writing to himself, in real time, while the negotiations were happening.

The plaintiffs' reading: the journal is a contemporaneous record of an intent to push Musk out and convert OpenAI to a for-profit while publicly maintaining a commitment to the nonprofit. Mr. Molo's recross frame: 'It's just an after-the-fact manufactured excuse for the very honest emotion that you expressed in the journal at the time.' The four entries that drive that reading: 'This is the only chance we have to get out from under Elon … take me to $1,000,000,000' (PX 151, Aug 21, 2017); 'Cannot say that we are committed to the nonprofit. Don't wanna say that we're committed if three months later we're doing B Corp, then it was a lie' (PX 161, Nov 6, 2017); 'It'd be wrong to steal the nonprofit from him. To convert to B Corp without him. They'd be pretty morally bankrupt' (PX 161); and 'It would be nice to be making the billions … We've been thinking that maybe we should just flip to a full profit' (PX 163, Nov 12, 2017).

The defense reading: 'morally bankrupt' refers specifically to voting to remove Musk from the board and then forming a B Corp without him — not to the for-profit conversion as such — and the 'only chance to get out from Elon' line is about saying no to Musk's unilateral-control demand. DX 1252, admitted Day 7 as a prior consistent statement under FRE 801(d)(1)(B), supplies the contemporaneous text the defense reading depends on: 'Real decision is fire Elon. … So we seem converged on the Fire Elon route.' On redirect, Brockman flatly denied ever committing to Musk that OpenAI would stay a nonprofit and described OpenAI Foundation's current ~$150–200B equity stake as proof that the mission survived.

The Court's role: the journal is an evidentiary problem because the same author writes both 'morally bankrupt' to convert to a B Corp without Musk and 'fire Elon' within twenty-four hours. Whichever reading the trier of fact adopts decides the case on trust formation and breach. The journal is also why the plaintiffs' equitable-remedies theory leans so heavily on documents the defendants themselves authored — the alternative is a case built on Musk's own credibility, which the cross-examination has already taxed.

sections.title: Robert Wu's 30(b)(6) deposition put the for-profit waterfall in evidence.

blocks.text: Until Day 7, the public record on the magnitude of value transfer from the nonprofit to the for-profit was largely inferential, with the OpenAI MSJ holding heavy redactions on insider economics. The Wu deposition, played for the jury, supplied the architecture in numbers.

Total target redemption across all limited partners — including Microsoft and the nonprofit — rounds to approximately $250B; the nonprofit's residual interest is not paid until those target redemptions are met. Microsoft's 2023 round was a $60B target on a $10B investment, a 6× return. The target redemption escalates 20% per year starting 2025. The 2023 second-amended Joint Development & Commercialization Agreement licenses Microsoft 'all IP and technology … excluding only AGI.' The Watershed MOU — non-binding — would let Microsoft reach product IP after a third-party-panel determination of AGI, eroding the AGI carve-out the 2018 Charter framed as protecting the public-benefit mission. As early as April–May 2024, OpenAI's 'mission strategy committee' began considering inverting the LLC waterfall into uncapped corporate stock. OpenAI Inc. — the nonprofit — has no full-time employees other than the board and Sam Altman as CEO.

On the legal questions in front of the trier of fact, the Wu numbers do three things. They put the disgorgement question in dollars (the equitable remedy the Court will size if liability is found). They give plaintiffs the actual-knowledge hook against Microsoft (an AGI carve-out is only worth negotiating if the parties understand AGI exclusion is a load-bearing feature of the original mission). And they establish that the for-profit pivot is not a hypothetical conversion contemplated for future capital needs — it is, on the corporate representative's testimony, an ongoing waterfall in which the nonprofit's residual interest is structurally last in line.

sections.title: Hon. Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers as case manager.

blocks.text: Gonzalez Rogers' rulings show three consistent commitments. First, evidentiary rigor over rhetoric: she rejected the antitrust theory because xAI 'admitted that it could not provide a single declaration from an investor'; she dismissed Section 8 standing because the alleged interlocks ended four months pre-suit. Second, doctrinal precision: she enforced California's agent-immunity rule on the for-profit subsidiaries, applied Cohen v. Kabbalah Centre on §17510.6, and refused plaintiffs' attempt to convert restitution into a charity redirect. Third, impatience with both sides: 'the parties to this action have repeatedly over-litigated this case'; 'The gamesmanship of both sides is obvious, as each flip flops.'

Her trial management has been notably hands-on: she struck Birchall's LOI testimony for lack of foundation; she sanctioned Toberoff for sending questions to a witness in real time; she set tight closing-time allotments (90/90/30); and she narrowed the case scope from the bench: 'This is not a trial on the safety risks of artificial intelligence… The question here is whether there was a breach of charitable trust.'

sections.title: What the record does not say.

blocks.text: Three categories of silence remain conspicuous, even with the trial record now substantially fuller. First, the insider equity arrangements beyond what Brockman and Wu have testified to: PX-350 disclosed a $10M Altman side-equity grant to Brockman in 2017 and Brockman conceded a ~$30B current stake acquired in 2018 for $0, but the Altman financial interests in the for-profit subsidiaries remain heavily redacted in the MSJ record.

Second, the November 2023 board episode: extensively framed by plaintiffs but only thinly documented in the public docket. Hoffman's corrected declaration in late September 2025 (#287) suggests the original December 2024 filing was inaccurate on something material; the public version does not say what. Toner's and McCauley's video depositions are scheduled but their substance is not yet in the public record.

Third, Musk's own donor-advised fund records: the OpenAI MSJ argues that Musk's contributions flowed through DAFs and YC.org, and therefore he has no settlor standing for restitution; plaintiffs argue the consideration is what matters and Musk should be treated as the donor in substance. The underlying DAF documentation was the subject of repeated discovery letter briefs but is not in the public docket. Whether Musk made the contributions personally or as a trustee of a DAF is one of the more important factual questions the trier of fact will resolve, and the public can see only the parties' framings of it.

The original complaint pleaded a kitchen sink — federal antitrust (Sherman, Clayton, Cartwright, UPA), Lanham Act false advertising, civil RICO, and a constellation of California fraud, contract, and trust theories. By the Jan 15, 2026 MSJ ruling, five claims survived. By Dkt #497 on Apr 24, 2026, fraud and constructive fraud were dismissed with prejudice. The live liability trial is now three theories: charitable trust, restitution/unjust enrichment, and Microsoft aiding-and-abetting.

What was added in the FAC (Nov 2024): Shivon Zilis as derivative plaintiff and xAI Corp. as competitor plaintiff; expanded antitrust theories. What was added in the SAC (May 2025): Aestas defendants restored; RICO §1962(c) repleaded with greater specificity. What was lost: Express contract (May 2025); Section 8 (Mar 2025); RICO entire (Aug 2025); derivative claims (Mar 2025); aiding-and-abetting fraud (May 2025); Lanham Act as to Musk (May 2025); implied covenant (Aug 2025).

What was added by OpenAI: counterclaims for UCL fraudulent/unfair prongs and tortious interference with prospective economic advantage, anchored in the February 10, 2025 LOI and its Wall Street Journal media campaign. The court allowed both to proceed to a Phase II trial; that phase is not part of the April 2026 jury proceedings.

sections.title: The filings that changed the trial.

blocks.text: The most important post-MSJ filings are not more founding emails. They are procedural and remedial: PTO #3 makes disgorgement equitable, PTO #4 bifurcates liability/remedies, Dkt #484 tries to remove Musk's personal financial interest, and Dkt #497 removes fraud and constructive fraud from the case with prejudice.

The proposed findings split the case three ways. Musk asks the court to find a charitable mission diverted and Microsoft knowingly assisting that diversion. OpenAI asks the court to find indirect unrestricted donations, no donor restrictions, no breach, and limitations. Microsoft asks the court to treat the founders' dispute as not its dispute, with no actual knowledge, no substantial assistance, limitations, laches, and unclean hands.

The statutory charitable-solicitation dispute is now explicit. Musk's §17510.8 brief says Altman's 2016 funding ask and the 2020 rent email created statutory trust duties; OpenAI's response says §17510.6 excludes member solicitations and that the 2020 email, even if relevant, was only a $580,000 rent-specific request already used for rent.

sections.title: What this site covers, and what it does not.

blocks.text: **Primary archive (court-case-md/):** 1,153 PDF-derived markdown files from the public docket, running through Dkt #522 filed May 3, 2026. The site treats docket filings as primary evidence and keeps trial-wiki material separate.

**Secondary commentary (case-files/):** trial-wiki pages from trial.mts.now documenting the proceedings of April 27 – May 5, 2026 (Days 1–7), including dedicated wiki pages for the Brockman journal and the Day 6 and Day 7 highlight digests. The trial-wiki is a parallel observation, not a primary docket filing. Quotes drawn from it are tagged as 'Trial' citations and link by transcript filename and line number; the site treats them as the most reliable available reconstruction of the courtroom record but flags them as secondary.

**Out of scope:** any post-trial motions, the verdict itself if it has been rendered, sealed exhibits not reflected in the public docket, and journalistic commentary outside the trial-wiki. The site avoids reasoning from press accounts when the underlying filing is available.
